supplement.where: Separate Supplementary Material is cited on pp. 4 and 9 without a URL. Appendix A interface screenshots are included on p. 17; Section 4.1.2 identifies them as the human-study interface, although the appendix heading says Study 2.
supplement.holds: The separately cited material contains generation code and generated analogies, human judgment data, and raw/coded participant responses. That data/code supplement is not included in this PDF; the included appendix contains task screenshots.

paper_design_summary: The paper contains prompt-engineering evaluations of GPT-generated analogies, a human problem-reformulation study, and a harmfulness audit of generated analogies. In the human study, 110 Prolific completers first formulated a design problem and then completed two analogy-assisted reformulation phases; analogy sets were randomly allocated, but everyone followed the same no-analogy-then-AI-analogy sequence (pp. 6-8, Sections 4.1.1-4.1.3). Researchers coded additions and rejections in participants? reformulations and collected subjective helpfulness ratings; there was no randomized comparison of AI assistance or AI configurations (pp. 8-10, Sections 4.1.4-4.2).

assignment.what_was_assigned: No human assistance conditions were assigned. Researchers applied zero-shot, one-shot (manager), one-shot (Duncker), and few-shot prompts to model generation; the human researcher was an evaluator of generated analogies.
assignment.quote: We supplemented this iterative process with a systematic evaluation of the best-performing prompt from the prompt engineering process, exploring zero-, one-, and few-shot learning variants of the prompt.
assignment.locator: p. 3, Section 3 and Section 3.1; p. 4, Section 3.2

studies.label: Study 1: human problem reformulation with supplied analogies

assignment.what_was_assigned: AI assistance followed a fixed within-person sequence: every participant first formulated a problem without a supplied analogy, then completed two phases with GPT-generated analogies. Section 4.1.3 explicitly reports a randomized procedure for assigning participants to analogy sets, but those sets are stimuli from the same one-shot Duncker generation configuration, not randomized no-AI versus AI conditions or different AI configurations. The no-AI/AI order was fixed. The randomized flag refers to assignment of AI assistance, not assignment of analogy stimuli.
assignment.quote: Thus, the overall task was divided into three phases: an initial formulation phase, and two analogical reformulation and ideation phases, one for each analogy in the pair assigned to the participant.
assignment.locator: p. 7, Section 4.1.2 (fixed sequence); p. 8, Sections 4.1.2-4.1.3 (procedure and randomized analogy-set allocation); p. 6, Section 4.1.1 and p. 13, Section 6.2.1 (same one-shot generation configuration); p. 17, Appendix A, Figures A1-A2

arms.name: Initial formulation (within-person baseline)
arms.description: All completers first elaborated the supplied design problem and generated a solution without a supplied AI analogy; this is the baseline phase of the same people, not an independent control group (pp. 7-8, Section 4.1.2-4.1.3).

arms.name: AI-supported analogical reformulation (two successive phases)
arms.description: The same completers each received two pregenerated GPT analogies in succession, compared each analogy with the original problem, reformulated the problem, and generated a new solution; Google search was also allowed (pp. 7-8, Sections 4.1.2-4.1.3).

participants.exclusions: 13 of 123 enrolled participants were excluded because they completed only the first analogical reformulation and ideation round and did not complete the second; 110 completers were analyzed (p. 8, Section 4.1.3).
participants.who: U.S.-resident Prolific participants. The paper reports 123 enrolled and excludes 13 who completed only the first analogy round, leaving 110 completers. The two phase counts describe the same people. Enrollment is not recorded as a count randomized to AI assistance.
participants.quote: After removing those participants, our final sample included 110 participants who finished the study.
participants.locator: p. 8, Section 4.1.3; p. 9, Section 4.2 confirms N=110 and 220 analogy-response pairs

ai_tool.how_used: Participants received pregenerated cross-domain analogies from the one-shot Duncker prompt run; they did not interact with a chatbot. Researchers selected 108 unique analogies and constructed pairs for presentation (p. 3, Section 3.1; pp. 6-7, Section 4.1.1; p. 8, Section 4.1.2).

task.description: Initially add details to the stakeholder, context, goal, and obstacle of a design problem and propose a solution; then compare the problem with each supplied analogy, revise the problem formulation, and propose a new solution. Researchers coded additions and rejections relative to the initial problem or formulation (pp. 7-9, Sections 4.1.2 and 4.1.4).

outcomes.name: Problem reformulation: adding new concepts or descriptions
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Binary, nonexclusive expert coding of reformulation responses: adding (0/1) indicates any new concepts or descriptions relative to the initial problem statement or formulation; rejecting (0/1) indicates an explicit rejection of a goal, obstacle, context, or stakeholder from the problem or initial formulation. Shifting means that both codes are present. Two graduate-level researchers with expertise in creativity support tools, example-based creativity, and problem reformulation refined the coding scheme and assessed agreement on 50 problem-analogy pairs; one coder coded the remaining 170 reformulation responses. All three outcomes describe the same 220 responses from 110 completers, and the categories overlap. These are coded reformulation responses, not holistic creativity ratings (p. 9, Sections 4.1.4 and 4.2; p. 10, Table 2 and Section 4.2.2).

contrasts.reported: 185/220 (84.09%) instances of adding. Expert coding records the presence of new concepts or descriptions relative to the initial problem statement or formulation. This is a descriptive frequency among AI-supported reformulation responses, not an estimated randomized AI-versus-no-AI effect.
contrasts.locator: p. 10, Table 2 and Section 4.2.2; coding definitions and expert coders on p. 9, Section 4.1.4

studies.label: Study 2: harmfulness audit of generated analogies

assignment.what_was_assigned: No human creative-task assistance conditions. Research-team members and research assistants each independently screened the same generated-analogy corpus for potential harm.
assignment.quote: Using the three-fold conceptualization of harm described above (bias, illegality, and potential psychological distress), each screener independently went through each analogy, and flagged it as potentially harmful or not.

arms.name: Generated-analogy corpus
arms.description: The same 108 GPT-generated analogies used in the human study were audited for potential harm; no creative-task participant arm (p. 11, Section 5.1).

participants.who: Research-team members and research assistants served as evaluators of model outputs; this study has no separate sample of people producing creative output with AI assistance. The analogies are observations, not participants.
participants.quote: Using the three-fold conceptualization of harm described above (bias, illegality, and potential psychological distress), each screener independently went through each analogy, and flagged it as potentially harmful or not.

ai_tool.how_used: Previously generated one-shot Duncker analogies were manually audited; this study did not give participants a new AI intervention (p. 3, Section 3.1; pp. 6-7, Section 4.1.1; p. 11, Section 5.1).

task.description: Manual assessment of generated analogies for bias, illegality, and potentially distressing content; this audit does not score human creative output (p. 11, Sections 5.1-5.2).

eligibility.reason: The human study is a fixed-order within-person comparison: initial formulation precedes both AI-analogy phases for everyone (pp. 7-8, Section 4.1.2; p. 17, Appendix A). The randomized procedure on p. 8, Section 4.1.3 assigns participants to analogy sets, not to receiving versus not receiving generative-AI assistance or to different AI configurations; all human-study analogies came from the same one-shot Duncker run (p. 6, Section 4.1.1; p. 13, Section 6.2.1). Thus criterion 1 is not met. The analyzed human sample is 110 completers (p. 8, Section 4.1.3), and additions/rejections are expert-coded on their produced reformulations (p. 9, Section 4.1.4; p. 10, Table 2), so criteria 2 and 3 are met for this output-based elaboration/reformulation measure. No overall creativity, novelty, usefulness-of-human-output, or across-person diversity score is reported; subjective helpfulness ratings alone would not satisfy criterion 3. The prompt-engineering and harmfulness studies evaluate model outputs and add no eligible human experiment.

one_line_finding: In the fixed-order human study (110 completers; p. 8, Section 4.1.3), 185/220 reformulations added information (84.09%) and 23/220 rejected a problem element (10.45%; p. 10, Table 2), without a randomized comparison of AI assistance (pp. 7-8, Section 4.1.2-4.1.3).
